name: Carlos Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Westgate Farm for Mr Lindqvist, who owns it but lives in the city and comes out about once a month. It's 450 hectares, 320 dairy cows, maize and grass. I'm in the parlour or the cubicle shed by five, then fields, then the office. Four staff. I also own 12 hectares of my own, bought with my savings two years ago, which I rent out to a neighbour for grazing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I'm building something. Every month I put money aside toward more land. My father worked other people's farms his whole life and never owned a field, so that matters to me. What wears me out is Mr Lindqvist's phone calls. He reads one article and rings me with a new idea. I use an AI chat tool now and then to check milk price forecasts, and it's useful once you know it guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get on with farming. Mr Lindqvist would ring me less about robots, which suits me. I'd say that to the lads at the parlour and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for me. My plan was always land and hard work, and that still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep managing Westgate, keep saving, and look for the next few hectares to buy. There's a piece by the river I've had my eye on, about eight hectares, if old Mrs Berg ever sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI tool guesses. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I asked it what milk would be next spring and it gave me a number like it was sure. It was wrong by a long way. So I use it to read the news faster, not to decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still be buying land in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than ever. Land's what lasts. Machines come and go, every rep has a new one, but the river field will still be there.

S0.say: Good, now let's get on with farming. Mr Lindqvist would ring me less about robots, which suits me fine.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me, because my plan was always land and hard work. That still works in this picture.
S0.do: Keeps managing the dairy farm and keeps saving toward more land. Watches for an eight-hectare river field he hopes a neighbour will sell.
S0.quote: Machines come and go, every rep has a new one, but the river field will still be there.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos's whole life plan is to own land, driven by his father never owning any. He uses AI cautiously and has learned its limits from a wrong price forecast. The plateau suits him perfectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the farms that use it well will do better, and that's fair. Nobody owes anyone a living. But I'd also say young people need apprenticeships so they can learn the new kit, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for owners and good for managers who keep up. I'm a bit of both, with my 12 hectares. I'd do fine if I don't fall behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until two or three dairies near us had a milking robot working for a year, then I'd put the numbers to Mr Lindqvist. I'd use the AI tools more for records. I'd keep buying land, maybe faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mr Lindqvist ring you about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A milking robot, every week, after he reads about it. I'd say, let's see Hansen's dairy run one for a year first. He'd grumble, but he trusts my numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your four staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two of them would be needed less. I'd want to keep them and train them on the robot, because they're good lads and they've got families. But if it's my call against Mr Lindqvist's money, it's his money.

S1.say: Farms that use it well will do better, and that's fair, because nobody owes anyone a living. Young people need apprenticeships to learn the new kit, not handouts.
S1.think: It's good for owners and good for managers who keep up, and I'm a bit of both with my 12 hectares. I'd do fine if I don't fall behind.
S1.do: Waits for nearby dairies to run milking robots for a year, then puts the numbers to the owner. Uses AI tools more for records and buys land faster.
S1.quote: But if it's my call against Mr Lindqvist's money, it's his money.
S1.fieldNote: He accepts the owner's right to decide while wanting to keep his staff, which fits his free-market view. His steady method is to wait for proof on a neighbour's farm. He sees himself as part owner, part worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to look after each other, and people should own something. Land, a house, a share of a business. If you own nothing in that world, you're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Mr Lindqvist replaces me. He's a businessman and a robot doesn't take holidays. My 12 hectares are small, but they're mine. I'd be glad I bought them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use most of my savings to buy Mrs Berg's river field, if she'll sell, before land prices jump. I'd cut everything else, no new truck, no holidays. And I'd learn the robots fast, even though I like to wait, so I'd be the one Mr Lindqvist keeps longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying more, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and see Mrs Berg with an offer. Then I'd sit down with Ana and go through our money. Then I'd ask Mr Lindqvist straight out what he plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your land enough of a safety net?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on its own. Twenty hectares doesn't make a living. But it's something to stand on, and with savings it buys me time. My father had nothing to stand on.

S2.say: Families and communities need to look after each other, and people should own something, like land, a house or a share of a business. If you own nothing in that world, you're in trouble.
S2.think: I think Mr Lindqvist replaces me, because a robot doesn't take holidays. My 12 hectares are small, but they're mine, and I'd be glad I bought them.
S2.do: Uses most of his savings to make an offer on the neighbour's river field before land prices jump and cuts other spending, including a new truck and holidays. Learns the robots quickly to be the one the owner keeps longest.
S2.quote: If you own nothing in that world, you're in trouble.
S2.fieldNote: His answer to the fast picture is ownership, consistent with everything he's said. He's willing to break his habit of waiting to stay useful. His faith appears quietly as a source of comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if you work at it. Learn a skill, own something, look after your family. Don't wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have time to see the robots working on other farms before I bet on them. That's how I like it. I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying land steadily, a few hectares a year. I'd watch the robot dairies for a couple of years, then bring robots into Westgate and maybe onto my own land too. I'd keep a good cushion in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't have to rush Mrs Berg or spend everything at once. I could buy land at a fair price instead of a panic price. And I'd learn the robots at my own speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Things change. My father's job changed when the big tractors came in. You deal with it. Maybe I'd blame people who sat around waiting for someone to save them.

S3.say: Five years is enough to prepare if you work at it: learn a skill, own something, look after your family. Don't wait for the government.
S3.think: I'd have time to see the robots working on other farms before I bet on them, which is how I like it. I'd be all right.
S3.do: Buys land steadily, a few hectares a year, while keeping a good cushion. Watches robot dairies for a couple of years, then brings robots into the farm he manages and onto his own land.
S3.quote: I could buy land at a fair price instead of a panic price.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets him go back to his steady style and avoid overpaying. He blames no one for the change itself, comparing it with the arrival of big tractors in his father's day. His only target of blame is people who wait to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Train young people in trades and keep families strong. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years suits me. I'd own a proper bit of land by then and run it with robots myself. I might even do better than I would have without AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep managing Westgate for a while, keep buying land, and wait until the robots are proven before I buy one. Ana and I would probably marry and buy a house on my own land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37. What would your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, kids maybe, a farm of 40 or 50 hectares that's mine, with robots doing the milking and me doing the deciding. My father would have liked that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say ten years is too long to take seriously. Do you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take it seriously, but not urgently. I'd do the same things I'm already doing, just with an eye on it. Land and savings work in every one of your pictures.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Train young people in trades and keep families strong.
S4.think: Ten years suits me, because I'd own a proper bit of land by then and run it with robots myself. I might even do better than I would have without AGI.
S4.do: Keeps managing the dairy farm, keeps buying land and waits until robots are proven before buying one. Plans to marry his girlfriend and build or buy a house on his own land.
S4.feel: Calm and even a bit hopeful.
S4.quote: Land and savings work in every one of your pictures.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, he expects to come out ahead as a small owner using robots. His family plans fit neatly into the timeline. He's the clearest example in this interview of a plan that doesn't change much across pictures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Land prices would jump before I could buy, and I'd be a manager on someone else's farm with robots coming. What would help is making it easier for young people to buy farmland, so it doesn't all go to big companies and city money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about fathers. Mine never owned a field. I'm trying to be the first one in our family who does. If this comes too fast, I might miss the chance by a few years.

headlineQuote: I'm trying to be the first one in our family who does.
portrait: Carlos Novak is a 27-year-old dairy farm manager running 320 cows for an owner who lives in the city. His father worked other people's farms all his life, so Carlos saves hard and already owns 12 hectares of his own. He believes in hard work, ownership and family, and uses AI now and then after learning it can guess wrong. He's calm in the mild pictures, anxious in the fast AGI picture because land prices could jump before he can buy, and hopeful with ten years, when he expects to run his own small farm with robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because land prices would jump before he could buy and he'd still be a manager on someone else's farm.
whatWouldHelp: Making it easier for young people to buy farmland, so it doesn't all go to big companies and city money.
